prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

EL PASO, Texas (CNN) -- The cell phone rang as Jorge Aguirre walked to a friend's funeral in Juarez, Mexico, last November -- a funeral for a fellow journalist who, Aguirre says, was assassinated for the critical stories he wrote. Mexican federal police recently began patrolling Ciudad Juarez, just across the border from El Paso, Texas. When he answered the phone, Aguirre heard a profanity-laced threat. "They told me I was next," Aguirre told CNN. "I thought they were going to kill me right there." Aguirre immediately gathered up his family and darted across the border into El Paso, Texas. He hasn't returned to Juarez since that day. Aguirre is seeking asylum in the United States, and he's part of a growing trend among Mexican citizens looking to escape the violence and corruption of their homeland.  Watch journalists met with death threats » . According to the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, an agency that falls under the Department of Homeland Security, the number of Mexican nationals requesting asylum in the United States based on "credible fear" has gone up every year since 2003, even as the overall number of "credible fear" asylum cases remains steady. In 2003, the USCIS reported 54 asylum cases from Mexican citizens. In 2008, that number reached 312. But asylum requests based on fear of violence aren't easy cases to make. Last year, the United States approved less than half of those cases. "Whether they're fleeing extortionists or potential kidnappers or they're leaving because of the drug cartels, it tells you there are definitely problems in Mexico right now," said El Paso Mayor John Cook. Those seeking asylum come from every walk of life. There are journalists, entrepreneurs and even law enforcement officials, including three police chiefs. For Raymond Cobos, the sheriff in Luna County, New Mexico, this is the most disturbing revelation. Just across the Mexican border is a dusty, far-flung outpost called Palomas, a speck of a town that's a popular path for drug trafficking and human smuggling. It's also been the site of wild gunbattles between cops and the cartels. The cartels outgunned the police force, and the police chief disappeared and sought asylum in the United States. It's not clear where his case stands or where the police chief is today. "I don't know what I would do. It's pretty hard to fight that type of situation by yourself -- if you're in an environment that you don't know from one day to the next if someone's going to knock on your door and blast your family away," Cobos said. Emilio Gutierrez is another journalist hiding in El Paso. He wrote stories critical of the Mexican government for a small newspaper in the northern Mexico state of Chihuahua, which shares a border with Texas and New Mexico.  Watch cops say U.S. teens were cartel hit men » . Last May, Gutierrez says men dressed in Mexican military fatigues raided his home in the middle of the night. He was told they were looking for drugs and weapons. A month later, a friend called, frantically urging him to hide. Gutierrez grabbed his family, drove to El Paso and requested asylum. He spent seven months in a U.S. jail as his case moved through the immigration system. He's recently been allowed to leave the jail while his request is pending. He's now in hiding in El Paso. "The fear never ends," Gutierrez told CNN. "We're scared for our families that are still on the other side, and we're scared for ourselves." Gutierrez and Aguirre offer a chilling perspective on everyday life in areas of Mexico that are consumed with violence and corruption. They describe a situation that has left ordinary citizens unable to trust anyone in positions of authority. "Thousands of families are in danger of being killed," Aguirre said. "They're vulnerable because they can't go to the police for help because that might get them killed."

**EL PASO, Texas (CNN) —** Jorge Aguirre was walking to a friend’s funeral in Juarez, Mexico, last November when his cell phone rang. The funeral was for a fellow journalist who, Aguirre says, had been assassinated because of the critical stories he wrote.

Mexican federal police had recently begun patrolling Ciudad Juarez, just across the border from El Paso, Texas. When Aguirre answered the call, he heard a profanity-laced threat.

“They told me I was next,” Aguirre told CNN. “I thought they were going to kill me right there.”

Aguirre immediately gathered his family and rushed across the border to El Paso. He has not returned to Juarez since that day.

Aguirre is seeking asylum in the United States and is part of a growing trend among Mexican citizens attempting to escape the violence and corruption in their homeland.

**Watch: Journalists face death threats »**

According to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, an agency within the Department of Homeland Security, the number of Mexican nationals seeking asylum in the United States on the basis of “credible fear” has risen every year since 2003, even as the overall number of credible-fear asylum cases has remained steady.

In 2003, USCIS reported 54 asylum cases involving Mexican citizens. By 2008, that number had reached 312.

However, asylum claims based on fear of violence are difficult to establish. Last year, the United States approved fewer than half of those cases.

“Whether they’re fleeing extortionists or potential kidnappers, or they’re leaving because of the drug cartels, it tells you there are definitely problems in Mexico right now,” said El Paso Mayor John Cook.

Those seeking asylum come from all walks of life. They include journalists, entrepreneurs and even law enforcement officials, among them three police chiefs.

For Raymond Cobos, sheriff of Luna County, New Mexico, that is the most troubling revelation.

Just across the Mexican border lies a dusty, remote outpost called Palomas—a tiny town that serves as a popular route for drug trafficking and human smuggling. It has also been the scene of fierce gunbattles between police and the cartels.

The cartels outgunned the police force, and the police chief disappeared before seeking asylum in the United States. It is unclear where his case stands or where he is today.

“I don’t know what I would do. It’s pretty hard to fight that type of situation by yourself—if you’re in an environment where you don’t know from one day to the next whether someone’s going to knock on your door and blast your family away,” Cobos said.

Emilio Gutierrez is another journalist now in hiding in El Paso. He wrote stories critical of the Mexican government for a small newspaper in the northern Mexican state of Chihuahua, which borders Texas and New Mexico.

**Watch: Police say U.S. teens were cartel hit men »**

Last May, Gutierrez says, men dressed in Mexican military fatigues raided his home in the middle of the night. He was told they were searching for drugs and weapons.

A month later, a friend called and frantically urged him to go into hiding. Gutierrez gathered his family, drove to El Paso and requested asylum.

He spent seven months in a U.S. jail while his case moved through the immigration system. He was recently allowed to leave jail while his request remains pending. He is now in hiding in El Paso.

“The fear never ends,” Gutierrez told CNN. “We’re scared for our families that are still on the other side, and we’re scared for ourselves.”

Gutierrez and Aguirre offer a chilling perspective on daily life in areas of Mexico consumed by violence and corruption. They describe a situation in which ordinary citizens have been left unable to trust anyone in a position of authority.

“Thousands of families are in danger of being killed,” Aguirre said. “They’re vulnerable because they can’t go to the police for help, because that might get them killed.”
outputs.L2:
EL PASO, Texas (CNN) — While heading to the funeral of a friend in Juarez, Mexico, last November, journalist Jorge Aguirre received a call on his mobile phone. The deceased was also a reporter and, according to Aguirre, had been murdered because of the critical articles he had published.

Ciudad Juarez lies directly across the border from El Paso, Texas, and Mexican federal officers had recently started patrolling the city. When Aguirre took the call, the person on the other end delivered a threat filled with obscenities.

“They said I would be next,” Aguirre told CNN. He believed he might be killed on the spot.

Aguirre quickly collected his family and fled across the border to El Paso. He has not gone back to Juarez since. Now applying for asylum in the United States, he is among an increasing number of Mexicans trying to escape violence and corruption in their country. A related video showed journalists discussing death threats.

Figures from U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, which is part of the Department of Homeland Security, show that applications by Mexican nationals seeking asylum on the basis of “credible fear” have risen each year since 2003. During that same period, the total number of credible-fear asylum cases has remained relatively stable.

USCIS recorded 54 asylum cases involving Mexican citizens in 2003. By 2008, the total had climbed to 312. However, claims based on fear of violence are difficult to prove. The United States approved fewer than half of such applications the previous year.

El Paso Mayor John Cook said that whether people are escaping extortion, possible kidnapping, or drug cartels, their departures clearly demonstrate that Mexico is facing serious problems.

Applicants come from many professions and backgrounds, including reporters, business owners, and members of law enforcement. Three police chiefs are among those who have sought protection.

Raymond Cobos, sheriff of Luna County, New Mexico, considers the involvement of police chiefs especially troubling. On the Mexican side of the border is Palomas, an isolated, dusty settlement frequently used as a route for drug trafficking and human smuggling. The town has also experienced intense shootouts between police officers and cartel members.

After the cartels proved better armed than local officers, the police chief vanished and applied for asylum in the United States. His present location and the status of his application are unknown.

Cobos said he did not know how he would respond under similar circumstances. He noted that it would be extremely difficult to confront such danger alone, particularly when someone could arrive at any moment and kill an officer’s family.

Another reporter sheltering in El Paso is Emilio Gutierrez. He worked for a small newspaper in Chihuahua, the northern Mexican state bordering both Texas and New Mexico, and wrote articles criticizing the Mexican government. A related video reported police allegations that American teenagers had worked as cartel assassins.

Gutierrez said that in May, men wearing Mexican military-style uniforms entered his home during the night. They claimed to be searching for guns and drugs. One month afterward, a friend telephoned him in a panic and warned him to go into hiding.

Gutierrez took his family, drove to El Paso, and applied for asylum. While immigration authorities processed his case, he remained in a U.S. jail for seven months. He was later released while his application was still under review and is now concealed somewhere in El Paso.

Gutierrez told CNN that the anxiety is constant. He and others fear both for themselves and for relatives who remain in Mexico.

The experiences described by Gutierrez and Aguirre provide a disturbing picture of daily life in Mexican regions overwhelmed by corruption and bloodshed. According to them, conditions have become so severe that ordinary residents no longer feel able to rely on people in authority.

Aguirre said thousands of families could be murdered. In his view, they are defenseless because asking the police for assistance may itself lead to their deaths.

Mexican journalist Jorge Aguirre fled Ciudad Juárez with his family after receiving a death threat while attending the funeral of a colleague who had allegedly been assassinated. Fearing for their safety, the family crossed into the United States, where Aguirre sought asylum.

His case reflects a broader rise in the number of Mexicans attempting to escape violence, intimidation, and corruption. U.S. immigration data showed that credible-fear claims by Mexican nationals increased sharply, from 54 cases in 2003 to 312 in 2008, even as the overall number of such cases remained relatively steady.

Despite this increase, obtaining asylum on the basis of violence remained difficult. U.S. authorities approved fewer than half of these requests, as applicants had to demonstrate not only that they faced a serious threat, but also that the persecution met the specific legal requirements for asylum.

Those seeking protection came from many sectors of Mexican society. They included journalists, business owners, police officers, and three police chiefs. The range of applicants underscored the broad impact of Mexico’s security crisis and the extent to which criminal violence and institutional corruption endangered both public officials and private citizens.
outputs.L4:
A growing number of Mexican journalists, public officials, and private citizens are turning to the United States for protection as violence, organized crime, and official corruption make it increasingly dangerous for them to remain in Mexico. Their asylum requests reflect not only the direct threat posed by criminal groups but also a deepening lack of confidence in Mexican institutions’ ability—or willingness—to protect people who report crimes, investigate corruption, or resist intimidation.

Journalist Jorge Aguirre’s experience illustrates the danger. After receiving threats connected to his work, Aguirre concluded that staying in Mexico could put his life at risk. Like other reporters covering organized crime and corruption, he faced a situation in which seeking help from local authorities might provide little protection and could even expose him to further danger. He therefore sought refuge in the United States, arguing that returning to Mexico would leave him vulnerable to persecution or death.

Journalists are not the only Mexicans making such claims. Police officers, government employees, business owners, activists, and other citizens have also crossed the border after being threatened by criminal organizations or after witnessing corruption. Some say they were targeted because they refused to cooperate with traffickers, reported criminal activity, or challenged powerful local interests. In many cases, the alleged involvement or complicity of public officials makes it difficult for applicants to find a safe place elsewhere in Mexico.

Federal asylum figures show that these cases increased sharply during the 2000s. The number of Mexican nationals making credible-fear claims rose from 54 in 2003 to 312 in 2008. A credible-fear finding does not itself grant asylum; it is an initial determination that an applicant may have a legitimate fear of persecution and should be allowed to present the case before an immigration judge. Even so, the increase suggests that more Mexicans believed the dangers at home were serious enough to justify seeking U.S. protection.

Winning asylum remains difficult. Applicants generally must demonstrate that they face persecution tied to a legally protected ground and that their own government cannot or will not protect them. Fear of widespread crime, however severe, is usually not enough by itself. Applicants must connect the danger to their individual circumstances and satisfy demanding evidentiary requirements. Fewer than half of the Mexican applications under discussion were approved, leaving many claimants facing prolonged legal proceedings, uncertainty, or possible return.

The trend is therefore significant even though the overall numbers remain limited and most applicants do not succeed. Rising credible-fear claims offer another measure of worsening insecurity in Mexico: people who once might have sought protection from their own institutions are increasingly asking another country to shield them. Cases such as Aguirre’s show how violence and corruption can erode not only public safety but also freedom of expression, confidence in government, and the ability of citizens to live and work without fear.

El PASO, Texas, is a vibrant border city known for its rich culture, desert landscapes, and close relationship with neighboring Ciudad Juárez, Mexico. As one of the largest cities along the U.S.–Mexico border, El Paso often plays an important role in national discussions about immigration, trade, security, and regional development.

Major news organizations such as CNN frequently report from El Paso when covering border policies and humanitarian issues. However, the city is more than a news headline. It is home to diverse communities, historic landmarks, renowned Southwestern cuisine, and a strong sense of local identity. El Paso’s unique position makes it an important place for understanding both Texas and the broader relationship between the United States and Mexico.

counterfactuals.output:
## As Violence Escalated in Ciudad Juárez, Some Sought Safety Across the Border

For years, Ciudad Juárez was defined by its factories, cross-border commerce and close economic ties to El Paso, Texas. But as fighting among drug-trafficking organizations intensified in the late 2000s, the city became one of the most dangerous places in the world. Journalists, business owners and senior police officials increasingly concluded that crossing the Rio Grande was their best chance of survival.

Reporters were threatened for identifying criminal groups, investigating corruption or simply covering killings. Newspapers reduced crime reporting, withheld bylines and practiced self-censorship after colleagues were murdered. Some journalists left Juárez entirely and sought asylum in the United States, arguing that neither local nor federal authorities in Mexico could protect them.

Entrepreneurs faced a different but related danger. Kidnapping and extortion became routine, with business owners ordered to make protection payments under threat of death. Shops and restaurants closed, while some proprietors relocated their families and businesses to El Paso. Those who had received direct threats sometimes pursued asylum, although applicants had to show that their persecution was connected to a legally protected ground—not merely that they were fleeing widespread crime.

Even police commanders were not immune. Officers and chiefs were targeted for resisting criminal organizations, cooperating with rival factions or attempting to reform compromised departments. A number of law-enforcement officials fled north after assassination attempts or threats against their families. Their departures illustrated the depth of the crisis: the people responsible for public security were themselves seeking protection abroad.

The violence coincided with a marked increase in asylum requests by Mexicans. According to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services figures reported at the time, **1,331 Mexican nationals applied for asylum in fiscal year 2003, compared with 2,487 in fiscal year 2008**. These USCIS numbers referred to applications rather than approvals; asylum remained difficult to obtain, and only a comparatively small portion of Mexican claims succeeded.

The flight from Ciudad Juárez therefore represented more than migration away from a violent city. It showed how sustained criminal intimidation could erode journalism, commerce and government simultaneously—and turn neighboring El Paso into a refuge for people who once formed the backbone of civic life across the border.
